name: YK-11
lead: YK-11 is a synthetic steroidal compound that is usually classed as a selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM). Wikipedia describes it as a gene-selective partial agonist of the androgen receptor that does not trigger the N/C interaction normally needed for full receptor activation, and as having anabolic activity in cultured C2C12 myoblasts greater than that of dihydrotestosterone (DHT).[1] It has been investigated in animal studies of sepsis-induced muscle wasting and has appeared on the market as a designer drug.[1]

The compound was reported by Yuichiro Kanno and colleagues at Toho University, Japan, around 2011, with a follow-up 2013 paper in Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin reporting that YK-11 increased follistatin expression in myoblasts, the basis of its marketing as a myostatin inhibitor.[2][3] Published work consists of cell and animal studies; no human clinical trial of YK-11 was found.[1]

YK-11 is not authorised as a medicine anywhere noted in the sources. Health Canada warned in 2022 that SARMs such as YK-11 are not authorised for any use and that bodybuilding products containing them can pose risks such as heart attack, stroke and liver damage.[1] It is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list and has been detected in doping control samples and in dietary supplements.[2][5][6]

paras: YK-11 has no approved medical use. Wikipedia notes animal investigation for sepsis-induced muscle wasting.[1] It is sold by online vendors as a research chemical and bodybuilding product, sometimes labelled myostine, and sometimes touted in bodybuilding circles as a potent myostatin inhibitor even though it remains experimental.[1][2] T Nation posters have described cycles with it alone or alongside other SARMs, GW501516 and andarine, and a mix that dropped RAD-140 for YK-11 and andarine.[7][8][9]

No studies found. No human clinical trial of YK-11 has been published.[1] Laboratory and animal research is described under Pharmacology and Research. A published case report documented detection of YK-11 in an athlete's doping control sample, which is an analytic finding and not a treatment study.[10]

Kanno's group found that YK-11 activates the androgen receptor as a partial agonist, promoting nuclear translocation without inducing the amino/carboxyl-terminal interaction that DHT induces.[1][2] In C2C12 myoblasts, YK-11 promoted myogenic differentiation more strongly than DHT, with the 2013 paper attributing this to increased expression of follistatin, a protein that binds and neutralises myostatin, a negative regulator of muscle mass.[3][2] A later cell study reported that YK11 up-regulates additional factors in cultured cells, and a 2023 paper reported that YK11 induced oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, which Grokipedia describes as occurring in the hippocampus.[12][13][2] These are laboratory findings and have not been shown in humans.

Grokipedia adds that YK-11 enhances osteoblast differentiation and Akt signalling in cell lines, and its chemical name describes a 19-norpregnane backbone, which is why some forum users and commentators say it resembles a steroid more than a non-steroidal SARM.[2][14][15]

Most pharmacokinetic work is from anti-doping research: mass spectrometric characterisation, equine metabolism after oral dosing (which detected the parent compound and phase I metabolites in plasma and urine) and detection in horse mane hair.[16][17][18] A validation study screening 60 dietary supplements purchased online in 2020 found undisclosed MK-677 and YK-11 in some products.[19]

Human safety data are absent. Health Canada states that SARM-containing bodybuilding products can pose serious risks including heart attack, stroke and liver damage, and that long-term effects are unknown.[1] One forum poster, replying to a user with health problems after SARMs, said YK-11's structure resembles an oral methylated steroid, and another poster reported side effects from a cycle that he said were not worth the modest results.[20][24]

YK-11 is a steroidal compound: according to Grokipedia, its chemical name is (17alpha,20E)-17,20-[(1-methoxyethylidene)bis(oxy)]-3-oxo-19-norpregna-4,20-diene-21-carboxylic acid methyl ester, molecular formula C25H34O6, with a molecular weight of about 430.5. Its orthoester group can hydrolyse in acid.[2] Grokipedia is AI-generated and was used only for these structural details, which should be checked against primary chemistry sources.

YK-11 was reported in 2011 by Kanno and colleagues, with a 2013 Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin paper on follistatin expression and myogenic differentiation.[2][3] Detection of the compound in doping samples and in supplements followed, with analytical papers appearing from 2017 onwards.[10][16][19]

Health Canada issued a 2022 warning naming YK-11 (myostine), and WADA lists SARMs as prohibited at all times.[1][5] The anti-doping literature includes a 2024 letter on detection of YK-11 in a doping control sample.[10]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, YK-11 is described as an untested SARM of steroid-like structure, a compound with serious potential, or a compound that did nothing for the poster; one participant said it did not give notable results and was not worth the side effects.[20][21][22][23][24] Another poster said a friend uses it because it shares a base structure with DHT, and a poster asked whether it is acceptable to combine every SARM including untested ones.[25][26]

timeline.event: YK-11 first reported by Kanno and colleagues, Toho University.[2]
Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin paper reports follistatin expression and myogenic differentiation in C2C12 cells.[3]
Mass spectrometric characterisation of YK-11 for doping control published.[16]
Supplement screening study detects undisclosed YK-11 and MK-677 in products.[19]
Equine metabolism and cell-model oxidative stress studies published.[17][13]
Letter reports YK-11 detection in a doping control sample.[10]

lore.intro: YK-11 is discussed on forums as a steroid-like SARM that supposedly acts as a myostatin inhibitor, with mixed user reports.[22][23][24]

claims.claim: YK-11 is a myostatin inhibitor that builds muscle beyond ordinary SARMs
claims.believers: Posters cite its follistatin-raising result in cells and describe it as having serious potential.[22][23]
claims.experts: The follistatin finding comes from cultured mouse myoblasts; no human study has tested YK-11, and Wikipedia describes it only as an investigational partial agonist.[3][1]

claims.claim: YK-11 is really a steroid, not a SARM
claims.believers: Users note its structure resembles an oral methylated steroid or has a DHT-like base.[20][21][25]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and Grokipedia both describe it as a steroidal SARM and a gene-selective partial agonist.[1][2]

claims.believers: One user said a cycle gave okay results; another said it did nothing.[24][21]

claims.claim: All SARMs, including YK-11, can be safely stacked
claims.believers: A poster argued that mild suppression seen with one SARM implies safety in combining all SARMs.[25]
claims.experts: Health Canada says the long-term effects of SARM products are unknown.[1]

claims.claim: Products sold as YK-11 are what they say they are
claims.believers: Some posters buy from supplement shops and rely on the owner.[26]
claims.experts: A supplement analysis found YK-11 present undisclosed in some products, so contents can differ from labels.[19]
